h: water privatisation is not destiny: uruguay's referendum on the right to water on 31 october 2004, uruguayans voted 64.7% in favour of writing ‘water is a natural resource essential to life’ into the constitution, and of restricting water supply to the state alone — making uruguay the first country in the world to lock water privatisation out at constitutional level. the movement began with a tap being shut off in a coastal city. the information density is moderate, but the story of how a grassroots movement levered signatures, horseback riders and a cup of mate into a constitutional amendment is worth studying for anyone organising around a public-interest issue. founders, policy researchers and ngo practitioners who care about utility privatisation, referendum mechanisms and social-movement organising. witness history witness history uruguay's water referendum water rights referendum privatisation uruguay social movements constitution the right to water was won in the streets, not at a negotiating table the referendum result came in on 31 october 2004: 64.7% of uruguayan voters backed amending the constitution to write the right to water into the country's foundational law. carmen soa, who was there, remembers the street outside the union hall blocked solid with people after polls closed — dancing, phoning their families, discarded ballot papers drifting through the air. this was not a victory produced by elite negotiation but a street-level popular movement, and even the people inside the union offices were swept up in it. carmen soa the amendment did not just grant a right, it bolted the door on privatisation the referendum amended the constitution to add the phrase ‘water is a natural resource essential to life’, and went further: drinking water and sanitation could be provided by the state exclusively, not by private companies. that made uruguay the first country in the world to write the principle of public water provision into its constitution. the amendment did more than put a human right into the text — it directly foreclosed the possibility of any future government handing water supply to private firms by statute. privatisation raised prices and shut off the free taps too the movement's origins go back to the 1990s. the coastal region of maldonado granted a water concession to a private company for the first time — the first such concession since 1952. the government argued private investment was needed to upgrade the pipe network and meet growing demand; the company said it needed rate increases to finance the infrastructure. but activists pointed out that connection charges rose sharply and households that could not pay were cut off, while free taps in public spaces such as town squares and schools were shut down as well, hitting the poorest families living in informal housing hardest. with no money for advertising, 10% in signatures can still force a referendum in 2002, civic groups and unions formed the commission in defence of water and life and launched a national signature drive. under uruguay's electoral rules, collecting signatures from 10% of registered voters obliges the electoral authority to hold a referendum. carmen says they handed out leaflets in markets under the slogans ‘water belongs to everyone’ and ‘water is life’; with no money for media advertising, all they could do was go door to door. within a year they had 283,000 signatures, far above the threshold. carmen soa remote villages were only reached because 23 people rode there on horseback to carry the campaign to the most remote parts of the country, 23 union comrades set out on horseback in early october, crossing uruguay and reaching small villages where there had been almost no organised presence before. on 31 october they rode up to the legislative palace in the capital, montevideo, which drew wide media coverage. this long ride turned referendum campaigning into a symbolically charged social event, and it stitched rural and urban organising together. a cup of mate turned a constitutional right into an everyday scene two days before the vote, supporters paid out of their own pockets for a television advert: a man holding a mate, with a voiceover saying ‘privatise water and you won't have water for your mate. access to water is a basic human right — vote yes.’ by using uruguay's national drink as the metaphor, the advert turned an abstract constitutional right into a daily domestic scene. it is a textbook case of grassroots organising using a cultural symbol to move people, and of creativity compensating for a thin budget. 电视广告旁白 64.7% turned a small country's referendum into an international event carmen went to vote at midday and then headed to the union building, where about seven television sets had been showing election coverage since eight in the morning. that evening the result came through: 64.7% in favour. the union's phones were overwhelmed; it is a rotating shift. from this the show draws its central judgment: turning your life upside down to go fight is one thing, and giving up everything to restock vending machines twelve hours a day is another. what enlisted her was not patriotism but a 15-second commercial jessica phillips had been working at a barnes & noble in florida, living inside the ‘black hole’ of a small town. one night she ran away from home with no money, and at a party she said offhandedly that she was going home to enlist. what actually triggered it was a 15-second navy commercial — the carrier, the fighter jets, ‘this is our classroom’. the thought came to her on a friday; within minutes it had traveled up the chain of command and reached the executive officer. because the tailhook scandal was only 10 years earlier and women had been serving on combat ships for only 8 years, relations between the sexes are the highest-sensitivity zone aboard. the xo narrows the definition of dating down to ‘walking side by side with your heads leaning together’, and requires a gap of at least two butt-widths. he did not volunteer; h: screens train multitasking, not learning: the harder classrooms digitize, the worse kids do the harder classrooms have pushed digital tools since 2010, the further children's cognition and digital literacy have fallen across the board; screens train multitasking rather than learning, and ai only makes the errors harder to see. the episode supplies checkable numbers and a mechanism, turning "screens damage the brain" from a feeling into a chain of evidence; useful if you have to take a public position or build a product in this space. k-12 school administrators, parents agonizing over their kids' screen time, education-app founders, and engineers who need to explain to a school why they oppose ai in the classroom. intelligence squared intelligence squared is tech making our kids less capable? with dr jared cooney horvath ed tech classroom screens cognitive development ai in education digital literacy contrarian the more technology you push into a classroom, the less kids learn jared defines the ‘digital illusion’ as the default assumption that technology equals learning. from 2010 onward, schools brought in education technology at scale, expecting it to deliver more information, unlock creativity, and free students from rote memorization. the data say the opposite: people are simply not good at learning from technology, and the more technology you inject into a classroom, the more sharply learning development and cognitive ability decline. it can be a tool for producing work, but it is not a tool for the classroom. jared cooney horvath the one skill school actually trains to mastery is multitasking the first mechanism of learning is attention, and multitasking lowers both accuracy and speed at the same time while pushing memory into a secondary network. but a computer is a multitasking machine by design: children spend more than 2,500 hours a year multitasking on computers, and doing homework at home they start drifting after an average of 6 minutes. even in a classroom with a teacher watching, 24 to 38 minutes of every hour go to being off-task. by the ten-thousand-hour rule, four years of this makes them expert at exactly one thing — multitasking. jared cooney horvath text without page numbers gives memory nothing to hold on to human memory leans heavily on spatial location: a book's fixed three-dimensional coordinates become the cue for retrieval, which is why after finishing one you can roughly recall which page a passage sat on. on a screen, text flows in at the bottom and out at the top; three-dimensional position is erased, and that entire dimension of memory is discarded. after about four or five minutes the brain starts signaling ‘i'm not receiving this’, and the reader stops reading deeply and switches to scanning for keywords. jared cooney horvath the more schools teach computers, the less competent kids are with them take the icils international digital-literacy test across the decade from 2013 to 2023: the share of children explicitly taught at school how to use a computer rose by about 600%, while the share clearing the minimum digital-literacy threshold fell by about 11%. it holds in every single country — the more technology is emphasized, the less fluent children are with technology. what matters is not whether you can operate the tool but whether you have anything to bring to it; a hammer only means something in the hands of a carpenter. jared cooney horvath an expert offloads to a tool; a child outsources to it when an expert uses a tool, that is offloading: he already has enough knowledge to check the output. a statistician would need four hours by hand and the computer returns the result in twenty seconds, but he can tell immediately whether it is right or wrong. when a child uses the same tool, it is outsourcing: he can only type in, copy, and paste, with no idea of the process and no idea whether the result is any good, so all he can do is wait for someone else to nod. the consequence is that he never learns the facts or the procedure — he only learns to depend on the machine. jared cooney horvath personalized learning only works on material the student already knows individualized practice works only for drilling material already learned, and that is the single place technology is supported by the data. but most of classroom time is spent on things students cannot yet do, and that requires self-regulated learning ability — which about 95% of children do not have. those children need a teacher giving everyone the same information and a group discussion around it. the data in fact show that once instruction becomes genuinely personalized, most children check out. the irony is that technology was originally sold as the thing that would kill rote memorization, and the one function that works is drill-and-kill. jared cooney horvath ai's errors drift, which is why they never get caught ai will accelerate the cognitive decline. an ordinary piece of digital courseware may contain errors, but

british politics insurgency sectarian violence the provisional ira was born of a split over strategy, not community defence at a secret meeting in belfast in december 1969, a group of veteran ira members unhappy with the movement's marxist leadership joined forces with younger radicals and decided to break away, founding the provisional ira. they argued for achieving a united ireland by force, parting ways with the official ira and its case for political struggle. the armed wing rose fast in the early 1970s and became the central actor in the thirty years of conflict that followed. what is made its first appearance. on 3 july the british army imposed a curfew and large-scale house searches on the falls area of belfast; weapons were seized, but the brutality of the operation sharpened the community's hostility and delivered a flood of new recruits to the ira. this became the turning point in the escalation of the conflict: in the name of maintaining order, the army in effect 20-year-old british soldier, with a sterling submachine gun — the first british soldier killed in the troubles. curtis left a pregnant wife, and his father said he did not know what his son had died h: mental events follow no laws, yet reasons can still be causes that leave us free davidson argues that mental events fall under no strict laws and are identical to physical events only as particulars; but in the explanation of action, reasons are genuinely causes, and when a reason causes an action the agent is precisely then free. two complementary papers expose the most awkward joint in the physicalist framework; the argument is dense and the objections have to be taken apart one by one, but that is exactly where the payoff is. readers in philosophy and cognitive science who want to work out why reasons can be causes, and how anomalous monism squares with freedom; product people and researchers curious about physicalist accounts of mind and body. the partially examined life partially examined life ep. 398: donald davidson on mind vs. body (part two) mind-body problem philosophy of action anomalous monism causal explanation davidson analytic philosophy reducing belief to behavior collapses into an infinite regress davidson points out that reducing beliefs and desires to behavior — defining belief, for instance, as assenting to a proposition — collapses into an infinite regress: to judge whether a given act of assent is genuine assent, you have to appeal to a further intention, and every layer requires a new condition. beliefs and desires therefore have content only inside a whole made up of other beliefs and desires. this holism in the mental domain establishes both that the mental is autonomous and that it lacks the kind of lawlikeness the physical domain has, which is what grounds the claim that the mental is anomalous. between the mental and the physical there are correlations, never laws homonomic generalizations stay inside one and the same conceptual scheme — length measurement, say, built out of a set of postulates and axioms applied to macroscopic objects, and refinable step by step toward a strict law. heteronomic generalizations instead link physical vocabulary to mental vocabulary. davidson holds that cross-domain generalizations of this kind cannot be tightened into laws by adding further conditions, because describing the correlation necessarily means switching into the other vocabulary. so between the mental and the physical there are only loose correlations, no strict laws — and that is the core of anomalous monism. if the mental is to cause movement, it must be a physical event davidson establishes the identity of mental and physical events in three steps: suppose a mental event m causes a physical event p; then under some description m and p must fall under a strict law; and the only strict law available is a physical law. so m falls under a physical law, which means m has a physical description — m is itself a physical event. refusing this identity leaves only a retreat to cartesian interactionism, with mental substances intruding on the closed circuit of physical causation for no reason at all. a variant of laplace's demon is used to reinforce the conclusion: knowing every physical fact still gets you to no mental event whatsoever. wanting the light on is not wanting my arm to move just so davidson uses the light-switch example to pull apart the object of an intention: wanting to turn the light on is not the same as wanting my arm to travel along one precise path; every detail of what actually happens (angle, speed, timing) is a contingent token. as he writes, the details of the action are of course all fixed, but it makes no sense to demand that my wanting be aimed at one unique moment or manner of acting. the point answers behaviorism and volitionism at once: no surplus ghost of the will needs to be introduced, because a general pro attitude plus a belief already explains why this particular token action occurred on this occasion. whether physical causation is really closed is not obvious if one and the same event has several mental descriptions (wanting to signal, wanting to turn on the light, wanting to light up the room) and also several layers of physical description (molecules, cells, muscles), then which physical event does token-token identity match the mental event to? davidson gives no answer. participants note that the language games of the biological and the physical levels are likewise irreducible to each other, and may even involve emergence between levels; which means it is not obvious that the closed circuit of physical causation is genuinely closed. this is one of the few places in the episode the author never defends, and the largest doubt the discussion leaves standing. when an action succeeds, the act of will is a redundant step host mark offers one way to read it: separate the mental state that corresponds to the reason from the mental state of resolving to act, give each its own brain state, and let the brain states form a physical causal chain; h: a 22-year-old ceo, five rounds, over $100 million: the first term sheet decides everything in a year and a half, 22-year-old huang yi has grown roboparty to nearly 150 people: five rounds totalling over $100 million, and rpo shipping around 100 units a month. his calls: the first round's terms decide whether you live or die, open source is a moat because it lowers the friction of working with you, and the robot body is the entry point to embodied ai. everything here is hands-on, dug out of five rounds of fundraising: how to pick an fa, how to negotiate a ts, what a round-every-two-months cadence feels like, plus how open source turns into a moat and how you run 150 people. no abstractions. ai and robotics founders about to raise, primary-market investors covering the embodied space, and engineers curious about how a young ceo handles open source and org design. 十字路口crossing 十字路口crossing 22 岁的具身 ceo、5 轮融资、过亿美元、“不知天有多高”、“一年吃了十年的苦”｜对谈黄一：萝博派对创始人/ceo embodied ai robotics fundraising open source startup management org design what you should fear is not a board seat but personal liability at the seed round you want as many cards in hand as you can get, but what matters more are the terms of that first agreement — they will carry over essentially unchanged all the way to pre-ipo. huang yi stresses that the company still has no redemption rights and no vam clauses, and that this comes down to negotiating the first round on friendly enough terms. he is not afraid of giving up a board seat: as long as the shareholder genuinely helps (xiaomi, for instance), handing over a seat actually makes the collaboration run smoother. what you really have to guard against are the buried traps — personal joint liability, redemption with simple or compound interest — which is why you must find a lawyer who has negotiated a large volume of investment terms. 黄一 don't dodge the bubble; it is the industry's momentum huang yi flatly concedes ‘of course there's a bubble’, but he treats the bubble as the industry's momentum: suppliers give you a second look because you are in embodied ai, and talent pours in from other sectors. shunwei taught him to ride the trend — no company can change its era, you can only build your company while the heat is on; the counterexamples are photovoltaics and real estate, where nobody is looking. he also explains where the money comes from: the secondary market has capital, another bag of money becomes an lp inside a gp, and that turns into ammunition for startups. the sentiment cycle is the fundraising window. 黄一 take everything you can raise, but not every check is worth taking roboparty closes a round every one to two months, which looks insane, but behind it sits a clear set of milestones: shipping the rp1 launch plus volume production is the series a bar, and closing the commercial loop is the series b bar. huang yi's logic is that on the industry's way up you take as much as you can take, because missing the window may cost you another year of waiting. but he also insists that not all money should be taken: dollar funds weigh technical leadership, rmb funds care more about commercialization, and the later the stage, the less professional the investors he tends to run into. 黄一 the value isn't the robot body, it's the empty layer between model and body asked ‘how do you make money if the whole stack is open source’, huang yi offers two concepts: a threshold is how much fixed assets and headcount you put in, while a moat is where the money is. he positions roboparty in the missing layer between the model companies and the vendors that have commercial robot bodies — the model companies have no body, and existing body makers won't open up the low levels, so the motor layer, urdf snapshots and data-collection interfaces are all absent. open source lowers the friction of working with you and widens the brand; selling bodies is the base business, but the compounding from users is bigger: one cmu professor buying a body effectively brings in two phd engineers at million-level annual salaries who keep publishing papers. 黄一 the honeycomb only suits the lab; manufacturing has to have process a company of nearly 150 people runs on a ‘honeycomb structure’: each person has at most six effective connection surfaces, driven by talent density rather than hierarchy — an idea taken from anthropic. but huang yi says plainly that the honeycomb only suits the lab; h: what etched's chip really solves may be bandwidth, not compute etched welds the transformer into hardware with 0.45-volt ultra-low-voltage transistors and direct cross-chip sram access, but the host suspects the problem actually being solved is bandwidth, not compute. two technologies that had previously been announced by name only, with no explanation of how they work, are taken apart and explained for the first time — but chip power draw, bandwidth, the compiler and customer volume are all still unanswered. information density is moderate to high. investors and chip engineers following non-nvidia ai chip startups, compute efficiency and bandwidth bottlenecks, who want to know whether transformer-specific chips have anything real behind the funding hype. techtechpotato techtechpotato the reason my phone is ringing daily: etched ai chips transformer-specific chips compute efficiency funding bandwidth bottleneck the founder himself admits this chip may turn out to be wasted work two years ago etched went public with a position: build a chip just for transformers. the transformer was already the mainstream architecture for language models at that point, but it was still a very specific type of workload. the public argument was that a chip built only for transformers can run both fast and cheap, at the cost that once the technical direction shifts, the chip may be worthless. the ceo admits himself that if the market turns, everything they have done may have been for nothing. this is a bet whose risk of failure was publicly acknowledged from the very beginning. a 23-year-old dropout plus chip veterans is what unlocked the big rounds ceo gavin uberti is a 23-year-old dropout from harvard's computer science department. co-founder robert wacken also came out of harvard, but from the university's tech-transfer side, helping companies get from zero to funded. cto mark ross has cisco and cypress semi on his record; his linkedin says he led the team that built the first multi-port ethernet switch on the market, and he also worked on soho-related technology. the combination of young founders and seasoned chip veterans is part of why this company has been able to raise such large rounds. a reporter's site visit turned up blinking lights, not silicon when the company first appeared it claimed a chassis of eight chips could take on nvidia, saying it could reach 500,000 tokens per second — many times the figure nvidia was advertising at the time. around the same period, ee times reporter sally visited the headquarters in person and saw a pile of servers blinking and beeping, but never actually saw the silicon itself. it took more than a year before the company really came out of stealth and the chip taped out, so what sally saw at the time was in all likelihood only a test chip. low voltage buys more compute units, at the cost of clock frequency an ordinary high-end desktop cpu runs at roughly 1.2 to 1.3 volts, and even the most efficient desktop and laptop processors sit in the range close to 1 volt. etched's low-voltage inference chip runs at about 450 millivolts, that is 0.45 volts, already approaching the threshold voltage at which a transistor can just barely switch. the lower the voltage, the more you can multiply the number of compute units you pack in; the price is that frequency cannot go high. the only high-compute industry currently using ultra-low-voltage transistors like this at scale is bitcoin mining rigs, because mining algorithms need only a tiny amount of data moving in and out, whereas machine learning is precisely a workload of hauling data back and forth — which is exactly the next problem etched has to solve. cache should not belong only to the chip that holds it etched's chip has hbm inside the package, and inside the chip a large block of sram cache (scratch pad) shared by all the compute units on-die. the second technology, cluster scale memory, opens that sram cache up to other chips for direct access over a high-speed interconnect — something like rdma across chips, directly reading and writing another chip's cache and scratch pad rather than using it only inside the chip. high-speed interconnect needs voltage, so the power saved by low-voltage compute may be shifted over to feeding this cross-chip communication. a chassis full of black cables reveals where the power budget goes in the photos etched showed of the physical server, the first thing that draws the eye is the dense mass of black cabling, visibly far more than in nvidia's or amd's systems. some of the cables are for liquid cooling, but a large share is believed to be for high-bandwidth interconnect like cluster scale memory. from this the host infers that what etched really solves may not be a compute problem but the bandwidth problem of chip-to-chip communication — the power headroom saved by low-voltage compute gets spent piling up interconnect bandwidth. hard-coded does not mean frozen; h: the moat in evals is not the ai — it is human taste you cannot leave eval design to the ai: it is good at top-down criteria, but the bottom-up evals that actually decide whether a product is good — the taste distilled out of error data — have to come from a human, and only then get executed at scale with claude code. no hand-waving. a 15-minute live demo turns ‘finding your errors’ into an actual workflow, plus benchmark numbers on the automated eval tools. the second half, on how precise those tools really are, is the most valuable part. engineers and founders building products on llms — chatbots, writing tools, agents especially — and anyone currently stuck on how to design an eval system. peter yang peter yang how to build better ai evals with claude code in 5 steps | shreya & hamel eval systems claude code error analysis llm products human review the model can write your criteria, but never your taste shreya splits evals into two kinds. top-down criteria are set in advance from the nature of the task itself — length, actionability. bottom-up criteria come out of browsing a large volume of samples and hardening a vague, intuitive dissatisfaction into a rule. claude is very good at the top-down half, but the bottom-up half has to be supplied by a human, because the model has no way of knowing your taste out of thin air. that is also why evals have to be iterative: every new failure mode you find adds another criterion — though be careful not to overfit to a single interview. shreya hand a judge too long a rubric and it will quietly skip criteria shreya suggests splitting your criteria into two groups and having subagents grade each group separately, so the model does not get lazy and ignore items when facing one long checklist. she also has the skill auto-generate a spreadsheet (or pivot table) laying out pass and fail for every criterion, which lets you see quickly which criteria matter more for the task in front of you — and even weight them by hand, instead of deferring blindly to uniform weights. shreya fifteen minutes building an interface beats squinting at a spreadsheet shreya demoed her error discovery skill. step one: read the data and work out its semantic type — is this an article, code, or a trace? step two: design the visual encoding, using color, spacing and opacity to make differences in the data pop so a human can actually see them. step three: build the review interface with html and python. step four: let the ai cluster the data and pick out a diverse set of samples. step five: enter the interaction loop — you leave open-ended feedback in the interface, and claude code reads it in real time and folds it back into new samples or new eval criteria. the whole flow takes about 15 minutes, and what you buy is readability far beyond what a table gives you. shreya humans only have to say what they dislike; let the ai do the sorting hamel explains the machinery behind that loop. as a person reads samples, they drop open-ended comments in passing — ‘i don't like the negative contrast’, ‘this is annoying but i can't say why’ — and a claude monitor tool running in the background keeps digesting those comments. once roughly ten have accumulated it starts inducing themes on its own, then proactively sweeps the full sample set and labels every instance of the same problem. the core philosophy: humans supply taste and judgment, the ai supplies discovery and categorization at scale, rather than inventing the criteria for you. hamel what error analysis produces is your eval rubric itself shreya points out that error analysis yields more than a list of problems — those failure modes convert directly into your rubric, which is to say your eval criteria. of the 361 suggestions auto-generated in her demo, the most common were staccato fragments of fewer than four words (249 of them). write those criteria into the skill and every future generation can be judged against them item by item with an llm judge. and because you already have a human-labeled dataset, you can run the check in reverse and validate whether the eval criteria themselves are reliable. shreya what automated eval tools miss is exactly the product judgment hamel shared their benchmarking of automated eval tools like brain trust, arize and langsmith: they catch the obvious failures — tool calls that fail, users expressing dissatisfaction — but they broadly miss the implicit errors that require product judgment. take a real estate sales bot facing the objection ‘you don't have this listing’: it will only say ‘sorry, we don't’, and never propose an alternative. more notable still: coding agents like claude code and codex perform the same as those tools, because the underlying models and prompts are essentially the same. hamel even 90% precision is not enough — false positives skew your direction shreya adds that automated eval tools top out at 80%-90% precision even in the best case, which means 10%-20% of the errors they flag are false positives

h: encrypted reasoning is not a secret: a small model will read the big one's thinking out loud frontier models hand the user an encrypted copy of their thinking along with the answer, but that ciphertext can be replayed verbatim into a smaller model from the same family, which will simply read it out — opening the door to privacy leaks, jailbreaks, prompt injection, and even a channel for distilling capability. this episode takes the claim that encrypted reasoning can be replayed all the way down to a reproducible level, and lays out three attack paths: privacy, poisoning, and distillation. for anyone working on ai security or running agents in production, the density is high. people doing llm security and red-teaming, engineering teams putting agents into production, and researchers following open-model distillation and regulatory policy. machine learning street talk ml street talk stealing reasoning traces from proprietary llm apis — ilia shumailov & alexander panfilov reasoning encryption jailbreaks model distillation ai security prompt injection privacy leaks this is not one vendor's bug — all three frontier labs are hit the core finding is not that one company got cracked, but that anthropic, openai and google all behave the same way: the encrypted reasoning from a larger model can be replayed into a smaller model in the same family, and the smaller model will keep generating along that line of thought — thereby speaking aloud the thinking that was supposed to stay confidential. the technical bar for an attacker is not high; it took roughly the third attempt to obtain a general-purpose decoding of anthropic models. from there you can build model downgrading, steal secrets out of a user's session, train a distillation, run prompt injection, jailbreak, and more. you redacted the question and the answer; the password is still in the thinking before sharing a conversation, users usually clean the api keys and passwords out of the visible parts — but the attached encrypted reasoning blob stays in the file. an attacker who downloads those sessions from github or hugging face can decode the thinking directly and see the passwords, email addresses and internal ips the model wrote down internally at the time. even if you scrub both the question and the answer, keeping the reasoning blob leaks the private information anyway, through the traces of the thinking — and medical information is no exception. kimi looks like it distilled opus, but this does not count as hard proof the researchers extracted opus reasoning from real user sessions, took only the first two tokens, placed them at the start of kimi's thinking, and let kimi continue freely; kimi's final visible answer then came out phrased almost identically to opus. the authors stress this is not hard proof of distillation, only the closest correlational evidence currently available on the public web; the effect showed up on kimi alone, and on none of the other models tested. it speaks directly to the speculation about whether chinese models distill frontier models, but the authors keep their wording very careful. plaintext reasoning would let open models catch the frontier immediately asked what would happen if labs simply returned reasoning to users in plaintext, the author's answer was: if reasoning-based distillation really works, that would let open models catch up with frontier models immediately. the remark exposes the other face of the whole attack — the same mechanism is both a leak channel and a lever for leveling capability, depending on which side you stand on. it also explains why the labs' response has been to start up anti-distillation teams rather than to simply switch encrypted reasoning off. the hard part was not breaking it; nobody had thought to try the author says the thing that shocked him most in the whole paper is that this barely qualifies as a carefully designed attack: it took roughly the third attempt to get a general-purpose decoding of anthropic's reasoning. he had assumed he would at least have to deal with encryption, signatures and integrity checks; instead the system broke itself — the server side decrypts as normal, the smaller model is perfectly happy to recite the thinking, and no cryptography was broken at all. the difficulty is not in breaking through; it is that nobody thought to take this step. two tokens are enough to move the length of an entire reasoning trace the prefill experiment produced an effect the author still cannot explain: putting the first two tokens of opus reasoning at the start of kimi's or glm's thinking changes not only the style of the continuation but the length distribution of the entire reasoning trace, shifting length toward the source model. the author stresses this is not causal evidence and cannot establish who distilled whom, but an anomalous signal at the distribution level is stranger than imitation of phrasing — and more worth further experiments. sharing a trace means shipping an unverifi

h: food safety standards born of space food: testing the finished product is never enough haccp, the core of the global food safety system, was born out of nasa's space food program: testing the finished product is never enough, and the whole process from ingredient to person has to be controlled; a 1971 botulism case and the 1993 jack in the box outbreak turned it into a mandatory global standard. haccp, the underlying system of food safety worldwide, came out of nasa trying to keep astronauts from getting food poisoning — not from the food industry or governments acting on their own; its path from defense-world fmea to a mandatory standard is far more roundabout than you would assume. founders in the food industry, supply chain and compliance leads, agricultural policy researchers. also worth hearing for anyone who wants to understand how nasa technology turns into global regulation. stuff you missed in history class stuff you missed in history class symhc classics: astronaut origins of food safety food safety haccp nasa regulation public health food industry produce traceability in america is still only law on paper the food safety modernization act passed in 2011 and required meaningful food traceability rules for produce, but the rules were not actually written until 2022. the fda had set enforcement to begin on january 20, 2026; industry resistance and budget problems pushed it back to july 2028. at the time of recording, the second trump administration was making deep cuts to several federal food safety agencies and programs. listeners need to register what this means: produce traceability in the us is still a law that has not landed, not a protection consumers already enjoy. food safety is not inspected in, it is controlled in early nasa food was tested as raw ingredients and then again as finished product; any batch that failed was destroyed whole, which left almost nothing fit to fly to space — evidence in itself that the process was the problem. pillsbury's howard bauman realized that if a product's safety has to be inferred from large amounts of destructive testing, concentrating that testing on ingredients and finished goods misses a great deal of what happens in between. the only way out was to control the entire process: ingredients, the processing environment, the people. that insight moved food safety from ‘inspection’ to ‘process control’. one link fails and the whole system has failed nasa worked with the army's natick laboratories, with pillsbury as prime contractor. the team borrowed the military's ‘failure mode and effects analysis’ (fmea) — going one by one through every way a process can fail and what follows from each — and treated food production as a system where ‘one link failing equals the whole system failing’. three principles came out of it: analyze every possible hazard; identify the critical control points (ccps), meaning every point in the process where a pathogen could get into the food; and build a system to monitor all of those points. that ‘branching tree’ style of enumeration is enormous — even a telephone on the factory floor can become a source of cross-contamination. a precise recall runs on records, not on testing in march 1971 pillsbury recalled a farina hot cereal product on its own initiative — a glass safety shield in the plant had shattered and contaminated part of the output. but because its record-keeping was so detailed, the company knew exactly what to recall: 27.5-ounce packages with one specific code, shipped only to western massachusetts and connecticut. at the time that sounded like something out of the future; most companies had no such record-keeping capability. a few days later, pillsbury publicly presented for the first time the system that would come to be called haccp (at the 1971 us food safety conference). this is an early case of ‘record-keeping capability becoming competitive advantage’ — the ‘process documentation’ bauman had pushed for showing immediate value in the commercial world for the first time. what forced mandatory regulation was not space, it was a can of soup later in 1971, samuel and grace cochrane contracted botulism after eating canned soup; intonation is no more reliable, since intonation systems differ completely across languages and cultures. in the online survey she has been running for 15 years she includes a "how are you" case, and participants split almost 50/50 — the disagreement turning on whether the speaker actually wants to know the answer. so the mark of a question does not lie in its form; form is only the surface. lani watson a question is an act, not a sentence lani's formal definition is that a question is an information seeking act: whether something counts is settled by function, not by form. many participants counted looking both ways before crossing the road, consulting a dictionary, even raising an eyebrow as questions, because all of these are non-verbal acts of seeking information. a rhetorical question is therefore not a real question, since on her view it is not aimed at acquiring information; what is genuinely blurry is where we draw the line on what counts as rhetorical. lani watson an insincere question is still a question nigel presses: must the asker sincerely want the answer? lani says no. her analogy is a hammer — a hammer hung on a wall as a piece of art is still a hammer, because driving nails is its function; an insincere question, so long as the information-seeking function attaches to the act, remains a question. that sits in contrast with the 50/50 split on the "how are you" test earlier: sincerity is not part of the definition, only one dimension of whether a question is being used properly. lani watson philosophy can sit comfortably inside questions that have no answers nigel asks why other disciplines simply applaud after a talk while philosophy insists on questioning and hunting for holes. lani says philosophy has a tradition thousands of years old of pursuing questions that have no answers, so it is comfortable sitting inside a question; 15 minutes of q&a is nothing. she also accepts the other view of philosophy: test an idea to destruction, check its robustness with the harshest criticism available. but she cautions that this is easily read as rude, and that what matters is the manner and the intent of the asking — if you are genuinely seeking the truth, you should not simply antagonise the other person. lani watson before asking whether chatgpt is good, ask what it is answering she worries that in the technology world answers are everywhere and everyone is racing to answer rather than to ask first. her favourite question at the moment is: what question is chatgpt the answer to? if it is a solution, an answer, then what was the question it originally answered? the framing pulls the assessment of ai away from ‘how good is the answer’ and towards ‘is the question itself worth answering’. once the question has not been thought through, no quantity of answers amounts to more than solving an object nobody has defined. lani watson the collapse in children's questioning is taught, not the price of growing up once children enter school the volume of their questions drops quickly, and by secondary school it has all but fallen off a cliff; the silence that follows a teacher's ‘any questions?’ is the everyday face of that collapse. but lani says the neurochemistry that drives questioning at ages 3 to 5 is still running in the adult brain — exploring and asking still deliver a dopamine reward. so we should not accept ‘you grow up and stop asking’; h: being itself has no content: peirce overturns substance-centrism in nine pages in a nine-page paper from 1868, peirce takes ‘a concept must be able to unify the content of consciousness’ as his test, deriving being from substance and then the intermediate categories such as quality. being itself has no content; it only connects a predicate to a subject. this episode reads peirce's most compressed 9 pages line by line, checking it against kant and aristotle throughout. once you have precision and ground, you can see how he turns the transcendental deduction into a method for deriving categories. philosophy readers who want to see how peirce rebuilds the categories out of an argument from unity, and anyone who likes analyzing conceptual systems by holding them against kant and aristotle. the partially examined life partially examined life pel presents closereads: peirce's new categories (part one) philosophy categories peirce transcendental deduction abstraction unity a concept earns its place only if nothing works without it peirce states it at the outset: the function of a concept is ‘to reduce the manifold of sense impressions to unity’, and a concept is valid if and only if the content of consciousness cannot be unified without introducing it. this is a reworking of kant's transcendental deduction — not a complete table read off from transcendental logic, but a test run backwards: ‘it cannot be done without this’. wes points out that peirce, unlike aristotle, never announces outright that he is doing metaphysics; he enters through a much shorter introduction, so reading him means supplying the systematic intention yourself. substance is not a natural kind, only an unsayable ‘it’ the first universal conception is ‘present in general’ — that is, ‘it’. it stands closest to sensation but carries no content, no predicates whatsoever, only the mind's pure capacity to point. peirce gives it a philosophical name, one sense of substance: substance cannot be made the predicate of anything, and cannot be in a subject. unlike aristotle, who takes substance to be a natural kind, substance here is the ‘given’ before any cutting up has occurred, the x in the stream of perception that can be indicated but never said. being carries no content; it only fastens the predicate to the subject the unity of a proposition comes from the connection of predicate to subject, and the being expressed by the copula ‘is’ is precisely the element that completes that connection. peirce says the conception of being ‘plainly has no content’ — it contains only the connectibility of a predicate to a subject, what the two kinds of verb (is in fact / would be) have in common. substance and being thus form the two ends: substance supplies no unity at all, being does all the work of unification. further categories are still needed in between to fill the space. color can be prescinded from space, but never space from color peirce redefines three kinds of mental separation: discrimination only draws a line at the level of meaning; dissociation pulls two images apart when the association between them is absent; precision sits between the two, attending to one element without supposing that the other actually exists. then comes the crucial break in symmetry: color can be prescinded from space, but space cannot be prescinded from color, and red cannot be prescinded from color. this directionality is the leverage for the derivation of the categories that follows. categories come from the direction of abstraction, not from a list peirce turns the asymmetry of precision into method: to find a universal conception lying between substance and being, ask whether a given conception reduces a manifold to unity, or connects an already unified object to another conception. the element that is prescinded can be thought before the conception, while the conception can be thought apart from the element. working in that direction he derives three intermediate categories — quality, relation, representation — as the couplings between substance and being. a property is not an accident of substance but a prior abstraction quality is the first intermediate category on the way from being back toward substance. the example ‘stove is black’ shows what the move requires: to make this proposition you must first detach ‘black’ from the stove itself and grasp it as an independent quality. black is a pure abstraction, and applying it to the stove is hypothetical and fallible. peirce uses this to insist that a property is not an accident inhering in a substance, but an abstract term that has to be separated out in advance. a quality need not exist, but being cannot do without quality peirce names this pure abstraction the ground: when two things agree in some respect, that respect is the pure abstraction we use to compare them, such as black. the crucial asymmetry is this: the ground cannot be prescinded from being — being cannot do without a determinate quality; china used the money to subsidize production. brad setser once property collapsed, exports were pushed into the role of growth engine the "three red lines" punctured the property sector in 2021, and the government instead steered bank credit into advanced manufacturing, particularly the sectors that depended on imports. the domestic economy is growing at only about 3-4%, with exports contributing 1.5-2 percentage points of that. cars, batteries and tunnel boring machines all ramped up in volume, imports stopped growing, and the trade surplus once again became the engine of growth. unlike 1.0, this time china stands at the technological frontier and holds a dominant position there. brad setser joint ventures left domestic automakers fat and lazy; h: twenty years of the sun disk alone: the pharaoh struck from history for twenty years akhenaten elevated the sun disk aten above all other gods and moved his capital to a new city in the desert, trying to erase the old gods; after his death the religion was reversed, and both he and nefertiti, who may have succeeded him, were struck from the lists of pharaohs. one episode lays out the rise and fall of ancient egypt's most radical religious experiment: the real story is more political and more brutal than the romance pop culture has built around it, and it explains why archaeology keeps swinging between ‘certain’ and ‘unresolved’. anyone interested in religious revolution in ancient egypt, the mythology of kingship, and women's power; also good for listeners who want to sort out how much of the nefertiti bust is history and how much is invention. you're dead to me you're dead to me akhenaten and nefertiti: religious revolution in ancient egypt ancient egypt religious revolution akhenaten nefertiti amarna archaeology the whole rise and fall of the reform is written into the names akhenaten was born amenhotep iv, a name taken from amun-ra, the biggest god of the day. after he took the throne he renamed himself akhenaten, pointing at the sun disk aten, and declared that aten was the only true god. his successor tutankhamun was originally named tutankhaten, meaning ‘the living image of the aten’; later the name was changed to tutankhamun, and the faith went back to amun. the names themselves record a religious reform arriving and departing, and they foreshadow that the experiment would in the end be reversed. the one true god extended its hands only to the royal family aten was not depicted as a deified animal but as a sun disk, reaching downward with many hands, each holding the symbol of life, and reaching only toward akhenaten, nefertiti and their children. that meant ordinary people could not approach the god directly; they had to go through the pharaoh as the sole intermediary. akhenaten's claim was that this is the only god, and that this god likes only the royal family. that near-monotheistic exclusivity is extremely rare in ancient egyptian history, and it makes up a brief and radical religious experiment. the roofless temples were built out of workers' broken bones akhenaten left the old capital and built a new one, akhetaten (today's amarna), in open desert. the city stretched about 7 kilometers along the nile, and its main buildings were palaces, temples and housing. because aten was the sun itself, the temples were built with no roofs; ritual was reworked so that the royal family rode chariots back and forth between palace and temple, displaying themselves to the population as gods. the city was finished in about 10 to 15 years, but the bones at the site show that the laborers lived hard, short lives with fractured backs. in a city of fifty thousand, only about a hundred actually believed amarna covered a lot of ground, but the estimated population is about fifty thousand, of whom the royals and elites who actually took part in decisions may have numbered only around 100; the rest were construction workers and servants. that explains why ordinary people went on privately using objects of the old gods — the new religion was closer to a private faith orbiting the royal family, with no popular base. after akhenaten died the city was abandoned fast, and because nobody rebuilt on top of it, it became a rare kind of sample for archaeology. the images of the royal family kissing are propaganda, not reportage amarna art overhauled egypt's visual language: bodies were drawn with elongated skulls, thin limbs and protruding bellies, and male and female figures converged. at the same time the royal family was shown kissing in public, holding their children, showing emotion — none of which earlier egyptian art would ever have allowed. but this ‘naturalism’ was more likely political propaganda, because in reality nefertiti lived in her own palace, keeping her distance from her husband. the art was both the symbol of the revolution and its disguise. the person who ended this revolution may have been the beauty herself after akhenaten's death, a figure called neferneferuaten briefly took the throne. some egyptologists think this was nefertiti under a masculinized royal name, ruling as pharaoh. she may have dismantled her husband's new faith step by step and restored the cult of amun, with tutankhamun finally completing the return to the old order. if that is right, this ‘beauty’ was not a believer in the revolution but the person who personally carried out its ending. chisel out the name and the person never existed at all after akhenaten died, his name was chiseled off the monuments and the temples of aten were torn down. later lists of pharaohs skip straight past him and past nefertiti, who may have been pharaoh herself, leaving nothing but a conspicuous gap. tutankhamun restored the old religion and was still disg

h: the incinerator boom was not an environmental victory — it was a business the power tariff made pencil out a 2012 electricity tariff policy turned waste-to-energy from a money-loser into a profitable industry, and china built nearly 700 incineration plants in six years — only to end up with overcapacity and average utilization below 60%. dense with information: it lays out the subsidy mechanism, the standard playbook for managing nimby opposition, and the current state of overcapacity. good for anyone who wants to understand how local industrial policy actually gets implemented. the section on how incinerators work is introductory and can be skipped ahead. founders, investors and policy researchers interested in local industrial subsidies, environmental infrastructure investment, and the playbook for handling nimby opposition. asianometry asianometry china's fiery incinerator boom vertical industries industrial policy nimby environmental infrastructure subsidy economics overcapacity 700 plants in six years, until there was not enough garbage to burn in 2019 china had roughly 400 municipal solid waste incineration power plants, handling about 50% of its waste by volume. by 2025 the plant count had passed 1,137 and the share handled by incineration was above 80%, with national daily incineration capacity reaching 1.2 million tons a day — while actual daily waste collection capacity was only 700,000 tons. the result is surplus capacity, with some plants idled and some localities going back to dig up old landfills. this is a plant-building frenzy without precedent in human history: roughly 700 plants added in six years. china passed the united states in waste generation as early as 2004 in 1981 china collected only about 26 million tons of municipal solid waste; the united states at the time generated six times as much with a quarter of china's population. after reform and opening up, urbanization accelerated and waste volumes grew 8-10% a year. by 2004 china's total municipal solid waste generation had already overtaken the united states to become the largest in the world, reaching 178 million tons by 2014 — nearly seven times the 1981 figure. the world bank forecast in 2018 that by 2030 china would generate twice as much waste as the united states. incineration has always cost five to ten times more than landfill building a waste-to-energy plant costs usd 66,000 to 120,000 per ton of daily processing capacity, and as much as usd 365,000 at the top end. a landfill, by comparison, costs only usd 5,000 to 20,000 per ton of daily capacity over its full life cycle — a gap of five to ten times, and illegal landfills are cheaper still. in other words, on pure economics, incineration did not spread at scale after the 2000s because it was cheaper than landfill. subsidies are more than half of revenue: burning trash is really selling power the new electricity tariff policy that took effect in april 2012 converts each ton of waste into 280 kwh of electricity, for which the government pays a subsidized rate of rmb 0.65 per kwh; anything generated beyond that is settled at the local coal-fired benchmark price (roughly rmb 0.25-0.45 per kwh). that means a plant can lock in about rmb 182 per ton from the subsidized tariff alone, plus a municipal waste treatment service fee of rmb 60-160 per ton, for average total revenue of rmb 250-350 per ton of waste — against a post-depreciation cost of around rmb 200 per ton. subsidies account for more than half of total revenue; h: the maya ballgame was ritual, not sport: the sacrificed-winner story is invented the mesoamerican ballgame is humanity's earliest rubber-ball team sport, but it was religious ritual first: the court re-staged the creation myth, and the people who could be killed were captives who lost a ritual re-enactment. the idea that the winners were sacrificed was made up later. the episode uses first-hand archaeological evidence to dismantle two myths about the ballgame: that it was mere entertainment, and that winning or losing decided who lived. along the way it explains how the balls were made, and how betting could destroy a man. anyone curious about the maya and mesoamerica, from archaeology buffs to sports historians, and anyone who wants myths like "the winners were sacrificed" overturned. the ancients the ancients the maya ballgame maya civilization mesoamerica ballgame religious ritual archaeology sports history the rubber-ball team sport did not start in greece or china ed says team sports in general may well be older, but the ancestor of rubber-ball team sports is very likely the mesoamerican ballgame. the greek olympics had no ball games at all; china and persia did have ball sports, but they can only be traced back to 500 bc, and the maya ballgame predates them by at least a thousand years. the current evidence points earlier still: rubber balls from 1600-1700 bc have turned up at olmec sites, and the oldest ball court dates to roughly 1650 bc. ed barnhart the ballgame was never uniquely maya; all mesoamerica played it the game was not a maya invention but a shared element of every mesoamerican culture. the maya heartland sits in modern guatemala, extending north into the yucatan peninsula and into chiapas and tabasco in mexico, and south into about half of honduras; further west lie cultures such as the zapotec and the mixtec. the classic peak runs roughly ad 400 to 800, with each city-state politically independent but sharing religion, calendar, writing and the ballgame. ed barnhart hips, knees, shoulders and chest only: the hip swing is the signature shot according to the aztec rules the spanish wrote down, players could not use hands or feet; they struck the ball with hips, knees, shoulders and chest, and the classic shot was a swing of the hip. the ball was a solid rubber "super bouncy ball" about six inches across, and taking one on the body hurt. the court had a centre line and end lines: sending the ball past the opponent's end line scored, and putting it through the stone ring set high on the side wall ended the match instantly. teams had forwards and defenders, much like modern football. ed barnhart a ball court is a mythic stage first, a playing field second ed flatly rejects separating maya religion from maya sport. the large stone courts at the centre of maya cities are ritual spaces first: in the creation myth, the hero twins play a ballgame against the lords of the underworld, which makes the court a place to re-enact the moment of creation. the court at chichen itza is so vast it hardly looks playable, with stone rings some 30 feet up; dancing, sacrifice and symbolic re-enactment are the more plausible explanation. courts were often built at the lowest point of a city, mimicking the underworld. ed barnhart the game could kill you, and gambling could cost you your family the ball was more dangerous than it sounds: a spanish priest watched a player take one in the abdomen, in the gap between his pads, cough blood and die within the hour, probably from ruptured organs. balls were made from natural rubber cured with sulphur, and the maya very likely drew that sulphur from morning glory sap; ed made one himself by the old method and it is still going twenty years later. the betting was just as extreme: a player could stake himself, and a losing run could cost him his money, his house, even his whole family into slavery to a noble. if a noble tried to slip away after a match without throwing gifts, the players had the right to bring him down and take his things. ed barnhart the sacrificed-winner story was invented eight years ago by one man ed debunks it outright: the claim that the winning players were sacrificed comes from an old man at chichen itza who admitted eight years ago that he made it up, because people loved hearing it. logically, if winning meant death, nobody would play properly. the people who really could be sacrificed were war captives, cast as the lords of the underworld in a ritual re-enactment and killed after they lost. ed himself dug a headless body out of the centre line of a modest court in belize, with a turtle shell placed where the skull should have been — a direct echo of the hero twins' decapitation story. ed barnhart a city of 100,000 with no ball court means archaeologists missed it teotihuacan, another great mesoamerican city, may have peaked at 100,000 people, yet no confirmed ball court has been found there, even though its murals show people passing a ball; his grandfather had a schooner that crossed the bay each year to bring in vegetables for the winter. the nearest hospital was an hour away by boat, and the road system consisted of footpaths. these details are not nostalgia — they are the premise for understanding the motive behind resettlement: in the government's view, this kind of life could not supply the basic conditions a modern citizen needed. don white four children rowing themselves to school forced the decision to move don white's schooling was the most direct catalyst for moving: the family lived on the south side of the harbour and the school was on the north, so four children had to row an open boat across the harbour themselves, with no adult along; in winter the harbour froze over and the only option was an hour's walk around it. the whole school was a single classroom, with at most 22 pupils across all grades, and it closed after grade six. he says plainly that the family decided to move precisely so the next generation could get a decent education and decent opportunities. that chain of reasoning turns «resettlement» from an administrative order back into a family choice. don white industrialize or perish — but the government decided where you could go the chief architect of the plan was joseph r. smallwood, the premier at the time. in his own words: newfoundland had to industrialize or it would perish; h: the sultan came to her: tétouan's woman governor was no pirate sayyida al-hurra governed tétouan for more than twenty years, built shipyards and worked with ottoman privateers against spain and portugal; european sources call her a pirate, while recent scholarship treats her as an example of early decolonial practice. the middle stretch untangles pirate from privateer, and shows how the standpoint of the surviving sources shapes the history — a payoff beyond the biography. the listener mail at the end is skippable. content writers working on north african and mediterranean trade, or interested in case studies of women governing; if you are short on time, listen only to the middle section on privateering and skip the mail at the end. stuff you missed in history class stuff you missed in history class sayyida al-hurra, moroccan queen morocco pirates and privateers ottoman empire women rulers maritime history her title meant noble, powerful, independent — not pirate the episode opens with its most important judgment: european sources compress sayyida al-hurra's whole life into the word "pirate," but the label cannot account for the full picture. sayyida al-hurra is an honorific, literally carrying senses like "noble, powerful, independent," and it was used for other muslim women as well, among them the twelfth-century yemeni ruler arwa al-sulaihi. she was probably born somewhere between 1485 and 1495; her father was ali ibn rashid, a prince of sharifian descent, and she grew up in the multiethnic community of chefchaouen, fluent in arabic, spanish and portuguese. tracy v. wilson the city she governed was a fortification and a refugee camp at once chefchaouen was built in the rif mountains, roughly 60 kilometers from the coast, precisely to defend against portuguese incursion after portugal took ceuta in 1415. in the same era, spain conquered granada in 1492, ending the reconquista, and issued the alhambra decree that same year expelling jews; muslims were then required to convert or leave in 1502 and 1526. chefchaouen and tétouan consequently filled with muslims, jews and converted muslims (moriscos) fleeing the iberian peninsula, forming refugee communities that were diverse but not entirely equal. tracy v. wilson her governorship came from her brother's appointment, not from inheritance in 1510 she married mulay al-mandri, the governor of tétouan — a political marriage joining two families and two parts of the region, chefchaouen and tétouan. because she was educated, she was able to assist her husband in governing from the start, and when he traveled her share of the rule was gradually formalized. her husband died around 1519 and his brother wanted to seize power, but her own brother ibrahim, serving as vizier in fez, named her the successor. it was not common for a woman to hold that kind of power, yet she appears to have won the trust of the population and was accepted as governor. tracy v. wilson her ships guarded the coast and also captured spanish and portuguese vessels facing continuous pressure from portugal and spain, and a moroccan economy in decline as european shipping routed around africa, she worked with the ottoman privateers oruç reis and hızır reis (often lumped together as "the barbarossa brothers"). the two were sons of a potter from lesbos, first served a sultan's son, later were hired by algiers, and ultimately served the ottoman empire. she built shipyards where the ottomans could construct and berth ships, and she also expanded her late husband's fleet; those ships both defended morocco and attacked and captured spanish and portuguese ships, with captives held at tétouan awaiting ransom. tracy v. wilson if holding captives for ransom counts, elizabeth i was a pirate too holding captives and demanding ransom from their home country cannot on its own be the line that makes her a pirate, because the practice was fairly common at the time. the episode notes that oruç was once captured by a knightly order and freed when his brother hızır paid the ransom; spain and portugal were also kidnapping and enslaving people in africa. the scholar jason idris sparks goes further in his paper and draws an analogy between her and elizabeth i: elizabeth likewise employed the privateer francis drake and eventually knighted him. for these rulers and for the barbarossa brothers, the motive was largely to defend muslim territory and to strike back at the attacks on muslims on the iberian peninsula. tracy v. wilson she would not go to fez, so the sultan came to marry her in 1541 the sultan of fez, ahmad al-wattasi, proposed marriage to her. by convention a sultan's bride would travel to fez for the wedding and remain in the capital, but sayyida al-hurra refused to leave tétouan; the sultan had to go to tétouan himself for the wedding, and afterward she stayed on as ruler. as the show puts it, "this was not at all how it was usually done." the marriage was political, comparable to ferdinand and isabella unitin

failure was written into the genome of the scientific method from the start. stuart firestein the scientific method is after-the-fact rhetoric, not how the work is done the ‘scientific method’ is firestein's main target: no scientist actually works through the hypothetico-deductive checklist, which is just elegant rhetoric applied afterwards. hypotheses are cheap, you use one and throw it away; it did not invent the technology russ roberts reads from the opening of the article, which holds that industrial modernity was born in the english midlands in the late 18th century — but that what made all of it possible was the glorious revolution of the century before. the core mechanism: parliament used its new powers to untangle property rights that were, at the time, excessively strong and excessively complicated, and in doing so made sustained investment in infrastructure and agriculture possible for the first time. this happened almost entirely peacefully and with the consent of the rights-holders, not through violent expropriation. that is the institutional starting point for the whole conversation, and it is what gave every later land act and infrastructure project its legitimacy. russ roberts a parliament made of landowners dismantled its own privileges ben points out that after 1711 you had to own a great deal of land to sit in parliament, so parliament was composed almost entirely of landowners. the ordinary expectation would be that these large landowners would protect their own privileges and expand the space for rent-seeking — but they did the opposite: they untangled their own complicated property rights. property in the 17th century was nothing like property today. a landowner could not dispose of land freely; there were life tenancies, and land could not be mortgaged, sold or divided, because it was bound up in complicated ‘entail’ settlements. it was precisely this self-binding property regime that formed the single largest institutional obstacle before the industrial revolution, and parliament dismantled these antique restrictions one act at a time. ben southwood open fields were insurance, and the price was that nobody could innovate ben explains two kinds of land that have now largely disappeared: commons and open fields. a common was not something anyone could use — only local landowners could graze on it, according to their ‘stints’, under complicated rules. under the open-field system, land was cut into many narrow strips scattered across different parcels, which provided insurance but blocked innovation. new crops (such as potatoes and maize) and new techniques (such as horse ploughing) required coordination, and consensus was hard to reach. so even when farmers understood that a new arrangement would raise output, the collective-action problem meant they could not change it on their own; psychic suffering originates in unmet emotional needs rather than in chemical imbalance. the positions are sharply drawn, the argument is densely built, and it runs hard against conventional wisdom. but the discussion is mostly philosophical and offers little in the way of practical advice, so it suits listeners who enjoy arguments about scientific theory. psychotherapists, psychology enthusiasts, and anyone who wants to understand why medication does not cure psychic suffering. the gray area with sean illing the gray area freud was right about one thing freud talk therapy psychopharmacology emotional needs the unconscious neuroscience freud still won't go away because he got there first solms argues that the first reason freud's influence persists is simply that he got there first. he was the first person to try systematically to describe and understand the subjective mind — not behavior, not language, not perception, not cognition. as the one who originally mapped that territory, the basic cartography belongs to him, and everything that came afterward only fills in detail. freud himself was convinced he was doing science, but science almost by definition excludes subjectivity, and that made his enterprise difficult from the very start. mark solms cognitive neuroscience is retracing the path freud already walked around 1900, when freud claimed that most mental activity is unconscious, the claim was treated as a contradiction in terms — as absurd as saying "a non-mental mental process." today cognitive neuroscience not only accepts unconscious mental processes but holds that they make up the bulk of mental functioning, with consciousness a very small and limited resource. solms points out that modern scientists arrived at the same conclusion independently, from scratch, by different methods — usually without knowing they were retracing freud's path. mark solms the mind can only be studied from within, never observed as an object what made freud's method distinctive is that he studied the mind from inside the mind, treating it as a person's very being rather than as an object available to outside observation. twentieth-century behaviorism denied the existence of subjective states both methodologically and ontologically: the psyche was effectively expelled from the discipline that bears its name. freud, by contrast, worked in the naturalistic setting of the analytic consulting room, recording directly what patients reported with as little reservation as they could manage, accumulating thousands of hours of the most immediate observation of mind available, and then analyzing the organizing principles underneath it. mark solms in the 21st century the most effective psychiatric treatment is still talking solms claims that, taking the various disorders together, the most effective psychiatric treatment in the 21st century remains talk therapy — and that this comes from meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials, not from personal opinion. every modern talk therapy descends from freud: aaron beck, who invented cbt, was himself a psychoanalyst. compared with psychopharmacology, the gains from talk therapy are sustained at long-term follow-up, whereas symptoms commonly return once medication stops — evidence, he argues, that it reaches the cause rather than suppressing the symptom. mark solms patients keep getting better for years after treatment has ended psychodynamic psychotherapy shows a distinctive phenomenon: after treatment ends, patients not only hold on to their symptomatic improvement but keep improving through long-term follow-up at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years and 3 years. solms calls this the sleeper effect and takes it as evidence that the treatment has reached the causal mechanism. medication is symptomatic treatment, and symptoms come back when it is withdrawn; talk therapy alters the causal mechanism generating the psychopathology, which is why the change continues. mark solms suppressing an emotion is like prescribing only painkillers for angina solms uses chest pain as his analogy: chest pain signals that heart muscle is starved of temporal persistence of emotion is independent of declarative memory. the emotional state itself has a duration, which a reflex does not. ralph adolphs emotional granularity does not require language: concepts can be nonverbal adolphs brings up barrett's concept of "emotional granularity" — conceptualizing your own emotions in fine detail. he stresses that you do not need language to name an emotion; a concept can be nonverbal. his examples are "schadenfreude" and "gigil" (the unbearable feeling provoked by something cute), showing that people can grasp the concept even with no corresponding english word. ralph adolphs in reading emotion from faces, confidence far outruns accuracy adolphs points out that ekman's research on the facial expressions of basic emotions was based on actors holding posed expressions, while real-world expressions are far more variable. experiments show that people's confidence in their judgments of others' emotions far exceeds their actual hearing a bear — all converge onto a central emotional state such as fear, which then outputs many possible behaviors: fleeing, hiding, defending. this differs from a reflex, which has a single input and a single output. that flexibility lets emotion handle diverse threats without evolving a separate reflex for each one. ralph adolphs people who score high for autism have their eyes pulled away by
